# Pronouncing Bhaiṣajyaguru: a guide for the curious

Saying **Bhaiṣajyaguru** aloud is harder than reading it on ​a screen, and more rewarding. The restored spelling is a compressed pronunciation guide: every accent and macron is an instruction. This post unpacks those instructions — the reconstructed sound, the phoneme-by-phoneme record, ‌the kindred forms in neighboring languages — and then zooms out to the full record around the name: its Devanagari writing, its mythology, its cult, and its modern life as a Unicode ‌domain. Whether you arrive as a linguist, a reader of myth, or a domainer, you will leave able to say the name the way the evidence suggests it was said — and ​able to type it the way it was written.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Bhaiṣajyaguru
- **ASCII form:** bhaisajyaguru
- **Meaning:** "Medicine master"
- **Domain of influence:** Healing, Medicine, Lapis-Lazuli Light
- **Pantheon:** Buddhist
- **Restoration:** Preserves ​distinctive marks
- **Original script:** भैषज्यगुरु (Devanagari)
- **Live domain:** bhaiṣajyaguru.com

## Overview

**Bhaiṣajyaguru** (*bhaisajyaguru*) — Healing, Medicine, Lapis-Lazuli Light · Medicine master — belongs to the Buddhist tradition, where it is catalogued under the ​domain "Healing, Medicine, Lapis-Lazuli Light". The name means "Medicine master".

**Bhaiṣajyaguru** belongs to the Buddhist tradition, where it is associated with healing, medicine, lapis-lazuli light.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Bhaiṣajyaguru** and ​serves its temple at [bhaisajyaguru.com](https://punicodex.com/bhaisajyaguru/). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode ​restoration exists. The plain ASCII form *bhaisajyaguru* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## ‌The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari as **भैषज्यगुरु**. Etymologically it means "Medicine master".

Sanskrit Bhaiṣajyaguru, from bhaiṣajya 'healing, remedy' + guru 'teacher'; the Medicine Buddha of lapis-lazuli radiance.

The ASCII ​form *bhaisajyaguru* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Bhaiṣajyaguru** recovers the full diacritic detail of ​the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one ‌historically valid Unicode restoration exists.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/bhaisajyaguru/** ​— Buddhist Reconstruction.

For the modern ​speaker, the closest approximation is: 'BHAISAJYAGURU' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

## Mythology

The stories of **Bhaiṣajyaguru** circulate within the Buddhist ​corpus, where the figure embodies healing, medicine, lapis-lazuli light.

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Bhaiṣajyaguru is attested in the canonical Buddhist sources as a figure associated with healing, medicine, lapis-lazuli light.

### Name and Meaning ‌(Etymology)

The name means "Medicine master" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Bhaiṣajyaguru**, the Medicine Buddha, presides over the pure land of Vaiḍūryanirbhāsa. He vowed to heal the physical and mental ​afflictions of beings and is invoked in healing rituals across Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna Buddhism. His deep-blue color and medicine-bowl emblem identify him in iconography. The twelve great vows of Bhaiṣajyaguru include the ‌promise to cure disease, relieve poverty, and guide beings toward awakening through medical and spiritual means.

### What He Promised Before He Was Buddha (The Twelve Vows)

The *Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabhārājasūtra* — in Xuanzang's Chinese ​translation of 650 CE (T. 450), the standard form in East Asia — first tells what the future Medicine Buddha swore as a bodhisattva: twelve vows. He would make his body shine ‌like lapis lazuli to dispel the darkness of ignorance; he would give beings 'inexhaustible' wealth of goods; he would set those on false paths on the bodhisattva road; he would restore broken ​precepts and heal 'bodies incomplete' — the blind, the lame, the deaf; he would cure the destitute sick and free the imprisoned from their chains; he would feed the hungry and clothe ‌the naked. One vow — that women who wish it be reborn as men — belongs to its century, and modern translators note it without flinching.

The list is the myth: a ​buddha defined entirely by his promises, and a definition of healing broad enough to include poverty, fear, and error along with disease.

### The World of Lapis Light (The Eastern Paradise)

Having fulfilled ‌the vows, Bhaiṣajyaguru presides over the eastern pure land the sutras call Vaidūryanirbhāsa — 'Pure Lapis-Lazuli Radiance'. Its ground is vaidūrya itself, transparent as glass; its avenues are bounded by cords of ​jewels; streams run through it sounding the teaching, and music plays without any musician touching an instrument — Yijing's longer translation of 707 (T. 451) spells the geography out in loving detail. ​There is no trace of the lower destinies — no hells, no hungry ghosts, no animal births — and beings in difficulty who hear his name and remember it are, the sutra ‌promises, rescued at the moment of death. Devotees who wish it may also choose rebirth in Amitābha's western paradise; the two buddhas are colleagues, not rivals.

If Amitābha's west is the sunset ‌of this life's grief, Bhaiṣajyaguru's east is its remedy: a paradise designed like a hospital, staffed like a pharmacy.

### How the Medicine Master Crossed Asia (The Translations)

The cult rode translation. Xuanzang ‌brought the shorter *Sutra of the Merit of the Original Vows of Bhaiṣajyaguru* back from India and rendered it in 650, fixing the Chinese name Yàoshī Liúlíguāng Rúlái — 'Medicine Master, Lapis-Lazuli ​Light, Thus-Come-One.' A generation later, in 707, the pilgrim Yijing translated a longer sibling text (T. 451), the *Sutra of the Seven Medicine Buddhas*, which surrounds Bhaiṣajyaguru with six other healing buddhas ​and preserves his healing dhāraṇī — a string of Sanskrit syllables still recited over the sick in Tibetan, Chinese, and Japanese monasteries. From China the sutra passed to Korea and, by the ‌early seventh century, to Japan, where the Medicine Master's name contracted to the two syllables every Japanese still knows: Yakushi.

A name's journey is the tradition's own map: Sanskrit to Chinese to ​Japanese in three generations, with the pharmacy intact at every border.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Bhaiṣajyaguru concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about ​the name:

- **Restored Name** — The Unicode form Bhaiṣajyaguru carries the original marks of the Buddhist tradition.
- **Source Script** — Attested in the original script as भैषज्यगुरु.
- **Domain** — Healing, Medicine, Lapis-Lazuli ‌Light
- **Etymology** — Medicine master

- **The medicine bowl** — Held in his left hand, it carries the myrobalan (harītakī) — the one attribute no other major buddha needs.
- **The myrobalan fruit** — ​The healing berry he offers, called in Ayurveda 'the remover of disease' — medicine as a concrete object, not a metaphor.
- **The eastern direction** — His pure land lies in the east, ​balancing Amitābha's western paradise — dawn against sunset.
- **Sun and moon radiance** — The bodhisattvas Sūryaprabha and Candraprabha attend him — light and its reflection as healing's witnesses.

**Bhaiṣajyaguru** does not stand alone. It ​belongs to the Buddhist tradition, where it is counted among 26 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — Healing, Medicine, Lapis-Lazuli Light — places it beside other figures who govern similar ​aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows ​**Bhaiṣajyaguru**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is ​a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Bhaiṣajyaguru** is one such vote.
